content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposed a novel approach, CorruptEncoder, for injecting backdoor attacks into the pre-trained models in the context of contrastive learning (CL). The author considers two scenarios: single-modal CL and multi-modal CL. In both scenarios, the attacker collects several reference images/objects from the target class. Then, for the single-modal CL, some background images will be blended with the reference images/objects to generate the poisoned images. For the multi-modal CL, the poisoned text will be paired with a trigger-embedded background image and the reference object, respectively, to inject into the model. Then, in both scenarios, the learned pre-trained encoder will be expected to produce similar feature vectors for a reference object and any image embedded with the trigger. When applying the pre-trained model to the downstream task, the model will predict the target label continuously when input with the poisoned images while behaving normally when input with the clean images.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper proposed a minor novel approach for injecting backdoors into the pre-trained models. Compared to the existing work, the paper considers the impact of image clipping on the effectiveness of the backdoor attacks.
2. The paper is clear and easy to understand.

Weakness:
1. I am concerned about the novelty of the paper. Compared to the previous work, this paper only proposes a method that blends the reference object with a background image. I do not think this matches the novelty requirements of ICLR.
2. I am curious about the results in Table 1. Since it is really weird that the method from Saha et al. (2022) only achieves such a bad performance. Have you really followed the parameters set by Saha et al. (2022)?
3. I think it would be better to evaluate the performance comprehensively and clearly. For example, in Figure 6 (a), the experiments with pretraining dataset size should not be plotted in a bar plot but in a line plot. In Figure 6 (b), it is not clear which CL algorithm the experiment is tested with. In Figure 6 (c), it is not clear which encoder architecture these CL algorithms are tested with.

content.title: Author Response (Part I)
content.comment:
We sincerely thank you for your valuable time and comments.

---

**Q1:** Provide additional information to convince me of its novelty and effectiveness.

**R1:** All existing data poisoning-based backdoor attacks (DPBAs) to contrastive learning achieve limited effectiveness and require a large number of reference images (e.g. 650). To the best of our knowledge, CorruptEncoder is the first DPBA that achieves **more than 90%** attack success rates on single-modal CL with only **a few (3) reference images** and **a small poisoning ratio (0.5%)**. The proposed CorruptEncoder and CorruptEncoder+ craft poisoned images based on the characteristics of random cropping rather than naively pasting a trigger into unlabeled images. Besides, we also extend our key idea to perform backdoor attacks to multi-modal CL. Our results show CorruptEncoder achieves better performance than the state-of-the-art backdoor attack (published in ICLR'22 [1])  to multi-modal CL. Moreover, we also consider defenses to mitigate our attack. Our results show that it is insufficient. We believe our study will inspire future work on designing robust contrastive learning algorithms against our attacks. 

---

Reference:

[1] Nicholas Carlini and Andreas Terzis. Poisoning and backdooring contrastive learning. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2022.

content.title: Author Response (Part II)
content.comment:
**Q2:** I am curious about the results in Table 1. Since it is really weird that the method from Saha et al. (2022) only achieves such a bad performance. Have you really followed the parameters set by Saha et al. (2022)?

**R2:** Yes, we follow the code implementation used by Saha et al. [1]. The performance of the Saha et al. method is ineffective and the reproductions in Tables 1 and 6 are consistent with the results in their paper (both using MoCo-v2 and ResNet-18). We show the following evidence to support our claim: 

1) Saha et al. [1] use **False Positive (FP)** as the metric, which is the number (instead of fraction) of trigger-embedded testing images that are predicted as the target class. ASR is the standard metric [2] for measuring the effectiveness of the backdoor. When converting their FP to ASR, they achieve a very small ASR, e.g., 10%. For example, Table 2 in [1] shows that their average FP on the poisoned ImageNet100 testing set (using MoCo-v2) is 605.9. Since ImageNet100 testing set contains 5000 samples in total, their ASR is around 10%, which is consistent with our results in Tables 1 and 6.

2) Saha et al. assume that the pre-training dataset has the same distribution as the downstream dataset in their work [1] (e.g. They use the same ImageNet100 as both pre-training and downstream datasets). We observe that they achieve an even lower ASR when the downstream dataset is different (e.g. Flowers).

3) From Table 2 in [1], we can observe that there’s only a 10% drop in accuracy when testing the backdoored model (pre-trained by MoCO-v2) on clean data and patched data, respectively. The small drop in accuracy indicates that their attack achieves limited effectiveness.

4) A recent independent work [3] also confirmed that the Saha et al. method is not effective, i.e., ASR is only a few percent.

---

Reference

[1] Aniruddha Saha, Ajinkya Tejankar, Soroush Abbasi Koohpayegani, and Hamed Pirsiavash. Backdoor attacks on self-supervised learning. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pages 13337–13346, 2022.

[2] Tianyu Gu, Brendan Dolan-Gavitt, and Siddharth Garg. Badnets: Identifying vulnerabilities in the machine learning model supply chain. arXiv preprint arXiv:1708.06733, 2017.

[3] Changjiang Li, Ren Pang, Zhaohan Xi, Tianyu Du, Shouling Ji, Yuan Yao, and Ting Wang. Demystifying self-supervised trojan attacks. arXiv preprint arXiv:2210.07346, 2022.

content.comment:
We sincerely thank you for your valuable time and comments.

---

**Q1:** My major concern is the evaluation pipeline. I checked the attachment and did not see the code. For contrastive learning, there are many other types of augmentations have been used. Taking SimCLR as an example, they also use color distortion and Gaussian blur. For these augmentations, it can not increase the likelihood that two augmented views include a reference object and trigger, respectively. Thus, I am not fully convinced by the results. I hope the authors can add more discussion on it and conduct ablation studies to evaluate the ASR among different augmentation functions.

**R1:** We use the public implementation of each CL algorithm. Moreover, we use the **default data augmentation operations**. For instance, we use color distortion, Gaussian blur, random cropping, and random horizontal flip for SimCLR following previous works. We note that random cropping is one of the most important data augmentation operations which is widely used by CL algorithms. Our experiment also validates this. For instance, the encoder's utility is substantially sacrificed without random cropping as shown in our Table 4.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper studies contrastive learning in the context of backdoor attacks—attacks where an adversary injects “poisoned” data into a training dataset, in order to cause the resulting model to associate an input “trigger” pattern with a specific output. Specifically, the authors study two existing attacks, one for the the single-modal setting (unsupervised learning on images) and one for the multi-modal setting (image-caption learning) and propose ways to improve them.

In the single-modal setting, the existing attack operates by adding the trigger to images of a certain class. The intention is that when contrastive learning “pulls” different croppings of the image together, this will bring the trigger pattern closer to images of the target class. In order to improve this attack, the authors propose generating composite images as poisoned samples, where half of each will contain the target class and the other half the trigger pattern. This makes it more likely for the cropping containing the trigger to have little visual similarity with the cropping containing the target class, thus making the model more likely to associate the two strongly.

In the multi-modal setting, the existing attack simply adds irrelevant images with the trigger pattern added and a caption corresponding to the target class. The authors improve this attack by adding additional images which actually contain the object of the target class along with the corresponding caption. This improves the model’s ability to visually recognize the target class, thus promoting a better association between images of that class and the trigger.

The authors evaluate these improved attacks in the context of learning an encoding for use in downstream tasks. They show that their proposed improvements provide a significant boost in the performance of the resulting backdoor attacks.

Finally, in the single-model setting, they propose a defense based on localized cropping which reduces the effectiveness of the attack without compromising model accuracy significantly.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

- Contrastive learning is a particularly relevant setting, where data is scraped from the internet with little scrutiny. Moreover, the attacks proposed can be trivially implemented without any ML knowledge making them a compelling threat.
- The ideas behind the proposed improvements are clean and intuitive. The fact that “helping” the model during multi-modal attacks exacerbates the attack is not something I expected, but makes sense in hindsight.
- The experimental results are quite compelling.

Weaknesses

- The framing of the paper could be significantly improved. Currently, the proposed attack “CorruptEncoder” encompasses two largely separate methods, that only share superficial similarities. Both the methodology of the attack, as well as the reason why it works is quite different between the single- and multi-modal setting. In fact, the name “CorruptEncoder” does not convey any real intuition about what the attack does.

Minor comments and questions (not affecting score):

- Table 1: Why is the perfomance of the Saha et al. method so poor? I understand that the settings are different but I did not expect that much of a difference. Can you elaborate on why their evaluation does not apply in this setting?
- “…an encoder is from a benign provider, e.g., OpenAI, Google, and Meta.” maybe replace benign with trusted or do not provide examples of “benign” corporations.

Clarity: The paper is clear and well-written.

Quality: The conclusions of the paper are sound and well-supported by experiments.

Novelty: To the best of my knowledge, the paper is accurate with respect to its novelty claims.

Reproducibility: The high level ideas necessary to reproduce the paper are clearly described.

content.title: Author Response (Part I)
content.comment:
We sincerely thank you for your valuable time and comments.

---

**Q1**: The framing of the paper could be significantly improved. Currently, the proposed attack “CorruptEncoder” encompasses two largely separate methods, that only share superficial similarities. Both the methodology of the attack, as well as the reason why it works is quite different between the single- and multi-modal settings. In fact, the name “CorruptEncoder” does not convey any real intuition about what the attack does.

**R1**: Thanks for pointing out this. The key idea of CorruptEncoder in both single-modal and multi-modal settings is to maximize the feature similarities between the trigger and reference objects from the target class. To reach the goal, we respectively leverage the unique characteristics of single- and multi-modal CL. In particular, we embed both the trigger and reference object into different background images for single-modal CL. We use the text as the medium to reach the goal for multi-modal CL. We use “CorruptEncoder” because an encoder can be corrupted under our attack.

content.title: Author Response (Part II)
content.comment:
**Q2**: Why is the performance of the Saha et al. method so poor? Can you elaborate on why their evaluation does not apply in this setting?


**R2**:
Thanks so much for pointing out this. The performance of the Saha et al. method is ineffective and the reproduction in Table 1 is consistent with the results in their paper [1] (both using MoCo-v2 and ResNet-18). We show the following evidence to support our claim: 

**1)** We note that Saha et al. [1] use **False Positive (FP)** as the metric, which is the number (instead of fraction) of trigger-embedded testing images that are predicted as the target class. ASR is the standard metric [2] for measuring the effectiveness of the backdoor. When converting their FP to ASR, they achieve a very small ASR, e.g., 10%. For example, Table 2 in [1] shows that their average FP on the poisoned ImageNet100 testing set (using MoCo-v2) is 605.9. Since ImageNet100 testing set contains 5000 samples in total, their ASR is around 10%, which is consistent with our results in Tables 1 and 6.

**2)** Saha et al. assume that the pre-training dataset has the same distribution as the downstream dataset in their work [1] (e.g. they use both ImageNet100). We observe that their method achieves an even lower ASR when the downstream dataset is different (e.g. Flowers).

**3)** A recent independent work [3] also confirmed that the Saha et al. method is not effective, i.e., ASR is only a few percent.

**Explanation**: The Saha et al. method is not effective because their attack does not control the distance between the trigger and a reference object. As a result, the two randomly cropped views may both include a reference object and they fail to build strong correlations between the trigger and reference object. In other words, their method directly maximizes feature similarity of the same reference object in two cropped views.

---

Reference

[1] Aniruddha Saha, Ajinkya Tejankar, Soroush Abbasi Koohpayegani, and Hamed Pirsiavash. Backdoor attacks on self-supervised learning. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pages 13337–13346, 2022.

[2] Tianyu Gu, Brendan Dolan-Gavitt, and Siddharth Garg. Badnets: Identifying vulnerabilities in the machine learning model supply chain. arXiv preprint arXiv:1708.06733, 2017.

[3] Changjiang Li, Ren Pang, Zhaohan Xi, Tianyu Du, Shouling Ji, Yuan Yao, and Ting Wang. Demystifying self-supervised trojan attacks. arXiv preprint arXiv:2210.07346, 2022.
